1) ECC is a powerful and flexible operation for encoding graphs and 2) graph matching is an effective tool for aligning predictions and ground truth in graph generation.

we have developed a novel convolution-like operation on arbitrary graphs, which is applied to the problems of encoding graphs and segmenting large-scale point clouds, and a method for generating variable-size graphs with an autoencoder, applied to molecule generation.

(1) Edge-conditioned Convolutions are a powerful tool to encode graphs with varying structure, (2) SuperPoint Graph is a useful intermediate representation for segmentation of large-scale point clouds and (3) GraphVAE allows us to decode variable-size graphs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how to transfer DL techniques developed for grid-structured data to graphs.
the development of DL architectures for graph data, which is an important direction in machine learning and computer vision.
the question of how to learn representations and perform inference on graphs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have successfully transferred the idea of convolutions to arbitrary graph data, which was a major obstacle for DL on graphs.
the graph structure is not a major obstacle for the application of DL methods.
the journey from graph to embedding and back has been made, but there is still a long way to go.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the applicability of graph-convolutions for encoding graphs, that we have proposed a new graph representation, and that we have introduced a new method for graph generation.
we have shown that it is possible to transfer the concept of convolutional filters to graphs, and to generalize autoencoders to graphs with varying numbers of nodes.
the graph domain offers a new and exciting challenge for DL, where the graph structure is not only a means of representation, but also a key factor for learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DL can be successfully applied to graphs directly, and the methods we introduce can be used as building blocks to construct DL architectures for graphs.
, while there are many differences between graphs and sequential or image data, the basic principles of DL are applicable to all domains.
DL on graphs is a promising research area, and that the techniques we propose are a first step towards a general-purpose solution.
